fields.Question: How many layers does the OSI reference model define?
fields.Hint: Count from Physical up to Application.
fields.Fact: The OSI model was published by ISO in 1984 as ISO 7498.

fields.Hint: Bits on a wire, fibre or radio.
fields.Fact: Cables, connectors and signal encoding all live here.
Ethernet switching happens at this layer.
Routers forward packets based on this layer's addresses.
Port numbers are a feature of this layer.
The Internet protocol suite has no separate layer for this.
Character encoding and data representation are its classic examples.
HTTP, DNS and SMTP are usually placed here.

fields.Question: How many layers does RFC 1122 describe for the Internet protocol suite?
fields.Hint: Fewer than OSI: link, internet, and two more.
fields.Fact: RFC 1122 names the link, internet, transport and application layers.

fields.Text: In the Internet protocol suite, IP belongs to the {{c1::internet}} layer.
fields.Extra: RFC 1122 layers: link, internet, transport, application.
fields.Hint: It sits between link and transport.
fields.Fact: RFC 1122 is titled Requirements for Internet Hosts, Communication Layers.

fields.Question: What is the unit of data at the data link layer called?
fields.Fact: An Ethernet frame ends with a frame check sequence.

fields.Question: What is a TCP unit of data called?
fields.Hint: Not a frame and not a packet.
fields.Fact: RFC 9293 uses this term throughout the TCP specification.

fields.Text: Wrapping data in a header for each lower layer as it moves down the stack is called {{c1::encapsulation}}.
fields.Extra: The receiver reverses it, stripping headers on the way up.
fields.Fact: An HTTP request over Ethernet carries TCP, IP and Ethernet headers in front of it.

fields.Question: At which OSI layer do Ethernet switches primarily operate?
fields.Fact: Switches learn MAC addresses by watching the source address of frames.

fields.Question: At which OSI layer do routers primarily operate?
fields.Fact: Routers decrement the IP TTL or hop limit on every packet they forward.

fields.Text: The largest packet a link can carry in one frame is its {{c1::MTU}}.
fields.Extra: MTU stands for maximum transmission unit.
fields.Hint: A three letter acronym about size limits.
fields.Fact: Standard Ethernet has an MTU of 1500 bytes.

fields.Question: How many bits long is an Ethernet MAC address?
fields.Hint: Written as six pairs of hex digits.
fields.Fact: EUI-48 is the IEEE name for this address format.

fields.Question: What is the Ethernet broadcast MAC address?
fields.Fact: Every station on the segment accepts frames sent to it.

fields.Question: What is the standard Ethernet MTU in bytes?
fields.Hint: Jumbo frames go well beyond it.
fields.Fact: Jumbo frames of around 9000 bytes are common but not part of the base standard.

fields.Question: Which EtherType value identifies IPv4?
fields.Fact: EtherType values are assigned by the IEEE Registration Authority.

fields.Question: Which EtherType value identifies IPv6?
fields.Fact: Hosts use it to hand the payload to the IPv6 stack.
Ethernet was developed at Xerox PARC in the 1970s.

fields.Hint: Splits one switch into many broadcast domains.
fields.Fact: The 802.1Q tag adds 4 bytes to an Ethernet frame.

fields.Text: An 802.1Q VLAN ID field is {{c1::12}} bits long.
fields.Extra: IDs 0 and 4095 are reserved, leaving 4094 usable VLANs.
fields.Fact: The tag also carries a 3 bit priority field.

fields.Text: ARP maps an {{c1::IPv4}} address to a {{c2::MAC}} address on the local network.
fields.Extra: Defined in RFC 826.
fields.Hint: Network layer address to link layer address.
fields.Fact: RFC 826 was published in November 1982.

fields.Text: An ARP request is sent as a link layer {{c1::broadcast}}, while the reply is normally {{c2::unicast}}.
fields.Extra: The requester does not yet know the target's MAC address.
fields.Hint: Who is asked, and who answers.
fields.Fact: Hosts usually cache ARP replies for a short time.

fields.Question: Which protocol replaces ARP in IPv6?
fields.Aliases:
NDP
Neighbor Discovery Protocol
Neighbour Discovery
ND
fields.Fact: It also handles router discovery and duplicate address detection.

fields.Question: How many bits long is an IPv4 address?
fields.Fact: That allows about 4.3 billion addresses in total.

fields.Question: How many bits long is an IPv6 address?
fields.Hint: Four times the size of IPv4.
fields.Fact: IPv6 addresses are written as eight groups of four hex digits.

fields.Text: CIDR stands for {{c1::Classless Inter-Domain Routing}}.
fields.Extra: It replaced class A, B and C addressing.
fields.Fact: CIDR was introduced in 1993 to slow routing table growth.

fields.Question: Which subnet mask matches a /24 prefix?
fields.Hint: Three full octets of network bits.
fields.Fact: Home networks very often use a /24.

fields.Question: Which subnet mask matches a /26 prefix?
fields.Hint: Two bits into the last octet.
fields.Fact: A /26 holds 64 addresses.

fields.Question: Which subnet mask matches a /30 prefix?
fields.Fact: A /30 was the classic choice for point-to-point links.

fields.Question: How many IPv4 addresses are in a /24?
fields.Hint: 2 to the power of the host bits.
fields.Fact: Traditionally 254 of them are usable by hosts.

fields.Text: RFC 3021 allows a {{c1::/31}} prefix on point-to-point links, using both addresses for hosts.
fields.Extra: No network or broadcast address is needed on such links.
fields.Hint: One bit shorter than a host route.
fields.Fact: It saves half the addresses compared with a /30.

fields.Question: Which /8 block does RFC 1918 reserve for private use?
fields.Fact: It holds over 16 million addresses.

fields.Question: Which /12 block does RFC 1918 reserve for private use?
Which /16 block does RFC 1918 reserve for private use?
fields.Fact: Consumer routers often default to 192.168.0.1 or 192.168.1.1.

fields.Question: Which block is reserved as shared address space for carrier-grade NAT?
fields.Fact: It exists so ISPs do not collide with customers' RFC 1918 networks.

fields.Question: Which IPv4 block is reserved for loopback?
fields.Fact: The whole block is loopback, not just 127.0.0.1.

fields.Question: What is the IPv6 loopback address?
fields.Fact: IPv6 reserves a single loopback address, not a block.

fields.Question: Which IPv4 block is used for link-local addresses?
fields.Fact: Hosts can pick these themselves under RFC 3927.

fields.Question: What is TEST-NET-1, the IPv4 range reserved for documentation?
Write 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001 in RFC 5952 canonical form.
fields.Hint: Drop leading zeros and collapse the zero run.
fields.Fact: RFC 5952 also requires lowercase hex digits.

fields.Text: IPv6 has no {{c1::broadcast}} addresses and uses multicast instead.
fields.Extra: For example ff02::1 reaches all nodes on a link.
fields.Hint: A feature IPv4 has and IPv6 dropped.
fields.Fact: Neighbor Discovery uses solicited-node multicast addresses.

fields.Text: In IPv6, routers do not {{c1::fragment}} packets; only the source host can.
fields.Extra: Paths rely on Path MTU Discovery.
fields.Fact: IPv6 moved fragmentation into an extension header.

fields.Question: What is the minimum link MTU, in bytes, required by IPv6?
fields.Fact: Every IPv6 link must carry packets of this size.

fields.Question: Which IPv4 header field is decremented by each router to stop endless loops?
fields.Hint: Its IPv6 counterpart is called hop limit.
fields.Fact: When it reaches zero the router drops the packet and may send ICMP Time Exceeded.

fields.Question: What is the size of the fixed IPv6 header in bytes?
fields.Fact: Extra features go into chained extension headers.

fields.Question: Which IP protocol number is TCP?
fields.Fact: These numbers are assigned by IANA.

fields.Question: Which IP protocol number is UDP?
fields.Fact: Firewalls often match on this field to filter UDP.

fields.Text: The DHCPv4 exchange is Discover, {{c1::Offer}}, Request, {{c2::Acknowledge}}.
fields.Extra: Often remembered as DORA.
fields.Hint: The server answers each client step.
fields.Fact: DHCP grew out of the older BOOTP protocol.

fields.Text: When several routes match, a router picks the one with the {{c1::longest}} prefix.
fields.Extra: Called longest prefix match.
fields.Fact: A /32 host route beats a /24 that contains it.

fields.Question: How is the IPv4 default route written in CIDR notation?
fields.Fact: It is used only when no more specific route matches.

fields.Question: How is the IPv6 default route written?
fields.Fact: Hosts often learn it from router advertisements.

fields.Text: A host sends packets for destinations outside its subnet to its {{c1::default gateway}}.
fields.Extra: The host still uses ARP or ND to find the gateway's MAC address.
fields.Fact: The destination IP in the packet stays the remote host, not the gateway.

fields.Question: Which protocol exchanges routes between autonomous systems on the internet?
fields.Fact: BGP sessions run over TCP.

fields.Question: Which TCP port does BGP use?
fields.Fact: BGP relies on TCP for reliable delivery of route updates.

fields.Text: OSPF is a {{c1::link-state}} routing protocol.
fields.Extra: Each router builds a full map of the area and runs shortest path first.
fields.Fact: OSPF uses Dijkstra's algorithm to compute routes.

fields.Text: RIP is a {{c1::distance-vector}} routing protocol.
fields.Extra: Routers share their routing tables with neighbours.
fields.Fact: RIP measures distance in hops.

fields.Question: What is NAT that maps many private hosts to one public IP by rewriting ports called?
fields.Aliases:
PAT
Port Address Translation
Network Address Port Translation
NAT overload
fields.Hint: It tracks ports as well as addresses.
fields.Fact: Most home routers do this.

fields.Text: Unsolicited inbound connections to a host behind NAT usually need {{c1::port forwarding}}.
fields.Extra: Without a mapping the NAT has no idea which inside host should receive the packet.
fields.Hint: A static rule on the router.
fields.Fact: This is one reason peer to peer apps need traversal tricks.

fields.Question: Which protocol lets a host behind NAT learn its public IP and port?
fields.Hint: A server reflects back what it sees.
fields.Fact: WebRTC uses it to find candidate addresses.

fields.Question: Which protocol relays traffic when direct NAT traversal fails?
fields.Fact: Relaying costs server bandwidth, so it is the last resort.

fields.Text: TCP opens a connection with {{c1::SYN}}, then {{c2::SYN-ACK}}, then ACK.
fields.Extra: This is the three-way handshake.
fields.Fact: Each side picks its own initial sequence number.

fields.Question: Which TCP flag abruptly aborts a connection?
fields.Fact: Connecting to a closed port typically gets this in reply.

fields.Question: Which TCP state does the side that closes first enter for twice the maximum segment lifetime?
fields.Hint: Busy servers can pile up thousands of these.
fields.Fact: It stops delayed segments from leaking into a new connection.

fields.Text: TCP flow control uses the receiver's advertised {{c1::window}} to avoid overwhelming a slow receiver.
fields.Extra: It protects the receiver, not the network.
fields.Hint: A field in every TCP header.
fields.Fact: The window scale option lets it grow beyond 65,535 bytes.

fields.Text: TCP {{c1::congestion}} control protects the network, while flow control protects the receiver.
fields.Extra: Defined for standard TCP in RFC 5681.
fields.Fact: Senders treat packet loss as a signal to slow down.

fields.Question: What is the sender side limit used by TCP congestion control called?
fields.Fact: The sender may have at most the smaller of this and the receiver window in flight.

fields.Text: During {{c1::slow start}}, the TCP congestion window roughly doubles every round trip.
fields.Extra: It ends at the slow start threshold or on loss.
fields.Hint: Despite its name, growth is exponential.
fields.Fact: Many stacks now start with an initial window of 10 segments, as described in RFC 6928.

fields.Text: TCP fast retransmit resends a segment after {{c1::three}} duplicate ACKs.
fields.Extra: It avoids waiting for a retransmission timeout.
fields.Hint: A small number of repeated acknowledgements.
fields.Fact: Duplicate ACKs suggest later segments arrived but one went missing.

fields.Question: Which congestion control algorithm is the default for TCP in Linux?
fields.Fact: It is standardised in RFC 9438.

fields.Text: The TCP {{c1::MSS}} option advertises the largest segment payload a host will accept.
fields.Extra: MSS stands for maximum segment size.
fields.Fact: It is only sent in SYN segments.

fields.Question: What is the usual TCP MSS over Ethernet with IPv4 and no options?
fields.Fact: With IPv6 the usual value is 1440.

fields.Question: What is the UDP header size in bytes?
fields.Fact: Source port, destination port, length and checksum.

fields.Text: UDP provides no {{c1::reliability}}, ordering or congestion control of its own.
fields.Extra: Applications add what they need on top.
fields.Hint: What TCP gives you that UDP does not.
fields.Fact: DNS, QUIC and many games run over UDP.

fields.Text: The UDP checksum is optional over IPv4 but {{c1::required}} by default over IPv6.
fields.Extra: IPv6 has no header checksum of its own.
fields.Hint: IPv6 dropped its own header checksum.
fields.Fact: RFC 6935 allows narrow exceptions for tunnels.

fields.Question: Which transport protocol does QUIC run over?
fields.Fact: Running in user space made QUIC easier to deploy and update.

fields.Text: QUIC uses {{c1::TLS 1.3}} for its handshake and key setup.
fields.Extra: Defined in RFC 9001.
fields.Fact: QUIC encrypts most of its packet headers as well as payloads.

fields.Text: QUIC avoids head of line blocking between {{c1::streams}}, because a lost packet only stalls the streams it carried.
fields.Extra: TCP delivers one ordered byte stream, so one loss blocks everything.
fields.Hint: Independent ordered flows within a connection.
fields.Fact: HTTP/3 maps each request to its own stream.

fields.Question: Which QUIC field lets a connection survive a change of client IP address?
fields.Fact: This makes switching from Wi-Fi to mobile data less disruptive.

fields.Question: What is the range of well-known ports?
fields.Fact: Binding them often needs elevated privileges on Unix.

fields.Question: What is the IANA dynamic or private port range?
fields.Hint: The top quarter of the space.
fields.Fact: Many systems pick ephemeral ports from here.

fields.Text: Clients usually connect from a short-lived {{c1::ephemeral}} port chosen by the operating system.
fields.Extra: The range depends on the OS.
fields.Fact: Linux exposes its range in ip_local_port_range.
SSH replaced Telnet for remote logins.
fields.Source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (https://www.iana.org/assignments/service-names-port-numbers/service-names-port-numbers.xhtml)

fields.Fact: Many ISPs block outbound traffic on it from home connections.
fields.Source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (https://www.iana.org/assignments/service-names-port-numbers/service-names-port-numbers.xhtml)

fields.Fact: Used over both UDP and TCP.
fields.Source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (https://www.iana.org/assignments/service-names-port-numbers/service-names-port-numbers.xhtml)

fields.Fact: Browsers assume it when a URL has no port.
fields.Source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (https://www.iana.org/assignments/service-names-port-numbers/service-names-port-numbers.xhtml)

fields.Fact: HTTP/3 uses UDP on the same port number.
fields.Source: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry (https://www.iana.org/assignments/service-names-port-numbers/service-names-port-numbers.xhtml)

fields.Text: A TCP connection is identified by source IP, source port, destination IP and {{c1::destination port}}.
fields.Extra: Together they are the 4-tuple.
fields.Hint: The last piece of the tuple.
fields.Fact: That is why one server port can serve many clients at once.

fields.Question:
Fill the blank in this Python TCP server.
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
s.bind(("0.0.0.0", 8080))
s.____(5)
conn, addr = s.accept()
fields.Hint: It marks the socket as passive.
fields.Fact: The argument is the backlog of pending connections.

fields.Question: Which socket call does a TCP client use to start the handshake?
fields.Hint: The server side counterpart is accept.
fields.Fact: A non-blocking connect returns before the handshake finishes.

fields.Question: Which transport does a SOCK_DGRAM socket in the AF_INET family use?
fields.Fact: SOCK_STREAM gives TCP instead.
One name can have many of them.
RFC 3596 is the current definition of this record type.
A resolver restarts the lookup at the target name.
Each one carries a preference number.

fields.Side B: Authoritative name server for a zone
fields.Fact: Parent zones use these to delegate child zones.

fields.Side B: Name for an address in reverse lookups
fields.Fact: Reverse zones live under in-addr.arpa and ip6.arpa.

fields.Hint: SPF and verification tokens use it.
fields.Fact: Domain ownership checks often ask you to add one.
Every zone has exactly one at its apex.

fields.Side B: Host and port for a service
fields.Fact: It includes priority, weight and port fields.
Public CAs must check it before issuing.

fields.Text: A name that has a CNAME record should not have {{c1::other}} record types, apart from DNSSEC records.
fields.Extra: This is why a zone apex usually cannot be a CNAME.
fields.Fact: Some DNS providers offer ALIAS or flattening to work around it.

fields.Text: A {{c1::recursive}} resolver performs the full lookup on a client's behalf, asking root, TLD and authoritative servers.
fields.Extra: Your ISP or a public resolver usually plays this role.
fields.Fact: Its cache is why repeated lookups are fast.

fields.Question: How many root server identities, a through m, exist?
fields.Hint: Count the letters a to m.
fields.Fact: Each identity is served by many anycast instances worldwide.

fields.Question: Under which domain do IPv4 reverse lookups happen?
fields.Hint: The address octets are reversed in front of it.
fields.Fact: 1.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa is the reverse name for 192.0.2.1.

fields.Text: A DNS record's {{c1::TTL}} tells resolvers how many seconds they may cache it.
fields.Extra: Lower it before a migration so changes spread faster.
fields.Hint: Same acronym as an IP header field.
fields.Fact: Some resolvers enforce their own minimum or maximum.

fields.Question: Which DNS response code means the name does not exist?
fields.Fact: RFC 1035 calls it Name Error.

fields.Text: Without EDNS(0), DNS messages over UDP are limited to {{c1::512}} bytes.
fields.Extra: Bigger answers set the TC bit and the client retries over TCP.
fields.Fact: EDNS(0) lets clients advertise a larger buffer size.

fields.Text: Among MX records, a lower preference value means {{c1::higher}} priority.
fields.Extra: Senders try the lowest value first.
fields.Fact: Equal values let senders spread load.

fields.Question: Which TCP port does DNS over TLS use?
fields.Fact: DNS over HTTPS uses ordinary HTTPS on 443 instead.

fields.Question: Which DNSSEC record holds a zone's public key?
fields.Fact: Resolvers check signatures against it.

fields.Question: Which DNSSEC record in the parent zone links to the child's key?
fields.Hint: It sits beside the NS records in the parent.
fields.Fact: It is a hash of the child's key, not the key itself.

fields.Question: Which RFC defines HTTP/3?
fields.Hint: Two after the HTTP/1.1 syntax RFC.
fields.Fact: It was published in June 2022.

fields.Text: HTTP/1.1 clients must send a {{c1::Host}} header in every request.
fields.Extra: It lets many sites share one IP address.
fields.Fact: HTTP/1.0 did not require it, which made virtual hosting hard.

fields.Text: HTTP/1.1 connections are {{c1::persistent}} by default.
fields.Extra: Send Connection: close to end one after a response.
fields.Fact: Reusing connections saves TCP and TLS handshakes.

fields.Text: HTTP/1.1 pipelining suffers head of line blocking because responses must return in {{c1::order}}.
fields.Extra: Browsers largely never enabled it.
fields.Fact: HTTP/2 multiplexing was designed to fix this.

fields.Text: HTTP/2 is a {{c1::binary}} framed protocol that multiplexes many streams over one connection.
fields.Extra: Each frame names the stream it belongs to.
fields.Fact: The request semantics are the same as HTTP/1.1.

fields.Text: HTTP/2 compresses headers with {{c1::HPACK}}, and HTTP/3 uses {{c2::QPACK}}.
fields.Extra: QPACK copes with streams arriving out of order.
fields.Fact: HPACK was designed to resist the CRIME attack.

fields.Question: Which TLS extension negotiates HTTP/2 during the handshake?
fields.Fact: It avoids an extra round trip to agree on a protocol.

fields.Question: Which ALPN token identifies HTTP/2 over TLS?
fields.Fact: HTTP/3 uses h3.

fields.Question: Which transport does HTTP/3 run on?
fields.Fact: HTTP/3 has no cleartext form.

fields.Question: Which response header tells browsers to use only HTTPS for a site?
fields.Hint: Known by a four letter acronym.
fields.Fact: Its max-age directive sets how long browsers remember it.

fields.Text: GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent, while {{c1::POST}} is not.
fields.Extra: Repeating an idempotent request has the same intended effect.
fields.Hint: The usual method for creating things.
fields.Fact: Clients may safely retry idempotent requests after a failure.

fields.Question: Which HTTP method does a CORS preflight request use?
fields.Fact: Browsers send it before some cross-origin requests.

fields.Text: Unlike 302, a {{c1::307}} redirect forbids the client from changing the request method.
fields.Extra: 308 is the permanent version of the same rule.
fields.Fact: Historically clients turned POST into GET on 302.
It is the most common response on the web.
Common for DELETE responses.
Search engines transfer ranking to the new URL.
Often caused by invalid syntax.
Servers may use it to hide a forbidden resource.
A Retry-After header may say when to come back.
It says nothing about the cause.
Reverse proxies return it when the backend fails.
It may carry a Retry-After header.

fields.Question: Which HTTP status code confirms a WebSocket upgrade?
fields.Fact: After it, the connection stops speaking HTTP.

fields.Text: A WebSocket opening handshake asks to switch protocols with the HTTP {{c1::Upgrade}} header.
fields.Extra: Its value is websocket.
fields.Fact: WebSockets over HTTP/2 use extended CONNECT instead.

fields.Question: Which header does a server compute from the client's key with SHA-1 and a fixed GUID?
fields.Fact: It proves the server understood the WebSocket handshake.

fields.Question: Which URI scheme means WebSocket over TLS?
fields.Fact: Plain ws defaults to port 80, the TLS version to 443.

fields.Text: WebSocket clients must {{c1::mask}} every frame they send to the server.
fields.Extra: Servers must not mask theirs.
fields.Hint: An XOR with a random key.
fields.Fact: Masking protects against cache poisoning of intermediaries.
event.data may be a string, Blob or ArrayBuffer.

fields.Text: A full TLS 1.3 handshake takes {{c1::one}} round trip before the client can send application data.
fields.Extra: TLS 1.2 needed two.
fields.Fact: The client guesses a key share group in its first message to save time.

fields.Question: Which RFC defines TLS 1.3?
fields.Fact: It was 28 drafts in the making.

fields.Question: What is the first message of a TLS handshake?
fields.Fact: It lists supported versions, cipher suites and key shares.

fields.Question: Which TLS message does the server send first?
fields.Hint: The server's reply to the opening.
fields.Fact: It picks the cipher suite and its own key share.

fields.Question: Which TLS 1.3 message proves the server holds its certificate's private key?
fields.Fact: It follows the Certificate message.

fields.Question: Which TLS message ends each side's handshake with a MAC over the transcript?
fields.Fact: It detects tampering with earlier handshake messages.

fields.Text: In TLS 1.3, every handshake message after the {{c1::ServerHello}} is encrypted, including the certificate.
fields.Extra: TLS 1.2 sent certificates in the clear.
fields.Fact: This hides which certificate a server presents from passive observers.

fields.Text: TLS 1.3 removed static RSA key exchange; certificate based handshakes use {{c1::ephemeral Diffie-Hellman}}.
fields.Extra: Written as (EC)DHE in the RFC.
fields.Fact: This gives forward secrecy for those handshakes.

fields.Question: Which TLS extension carries the hostname so a server can choose a certificate?
fields.Hint: Lets many HTTPS sites share an IP.
fields.Fact: It is sent in the clear unless Encrypted Client Hello is used.

fields.Question: Which TLS 1.3 extension carries the client's Diffie-Hellman public values?
fields.Fact: A wrong guess triggers a HelloRetryRequest.

fields.Question: Which extension does TLS 1.3 use to signal its real version?
fields.Hint: The legacy version field still says 1.2.
fields.Fact: This trick kept old middleboxes from breaking connections.

fields.Question: Which cipher suite must every TLS 1.3 implementation support?
fields.Fact: RFC 8446 also says implementations should support AES-256-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305.

fields.Text: TLS 1.3 0-RTT early data can be {{c1::replayed}} by an attacker.
fields.Extra: Only send idempotent requests as early data.
fields.Fact: HTTP has a 425 Too Early status for this case.

fields.Text: A server certificate is trusted when its chain leads to a trusted {{c1::root}} certificate authority.
fields.Extra: Servers send intermediates; roots live in the trust store.
fields.Fact: Root certificates are usually self-signed.

fields.Question: Which tool sends ICMP echo requests to test reachability?
fields.Fact: A host that drops ICMP may still be up.

fields.Question: Which ICMP type number is Echo Request?
fields.Fact: ICMPv6 uses 128 for the same job.

fields.Question: Which ICMP type number is Time Exceeded?
fields.Fact: traceroute depends on these messages.

fields.Text: traceroute finds hops by sending probes with increasing {{c1::TTL}} values and reading ICMP Time Exceeded replies.
fields.Extra: Each router that drops a probe reveals its address.
fields.Fact: Hops that do not reply show as asterisks.

fields.Question: Which protocol does classic Unix traceroute use for probes by default?
fields.Fact: It targets high, likely unused ports, starting at 33434.

fields.Question: Which tool prints DNS answers in QUESTION, ANSWER and AUTHORITY sections?
fields.Fact: It talks to the resolver from /etc/resolv.conf unless you pick one with @.

fields.Question: Which dig option follows delegation from the root servers?
fields.Fact: It does iterative queries itself instead of using a recursive resolver.

fields.Question:
What does this command print?
dig +short example.com AAAA
fields.Aliases:
IPv6 addresses
IPv6 address
AAAA records
fields.Fact: +short drops everything except the answer data.

fields.Question: Which command line tool captures packets using BPF filter expressions?
fields.Fact: Wireshark can open its pcap files.

fields.Question:
What does this command capture?
tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp port 443'
fields.Aliases:
HTTPS traffic
Port 443 TCP traffic
TCP port 443
fields.Fact: Either source or destination port can match.

fields.Question: Which iproute2 tool replaces netstat for listing sockets?
fields.Fact: It reads socket data from the kernel faster than netstat.

fields.Question: Which ss flag limits output to listening sockets?
fields.Fact: -t limits to TCP and -n skips name resolution.

fields.Question: Which iproute2 command shows the routing table?
fields.Fact: ip route get shows the route for a single address.

fields.Question: Which curl flag shows request and response headers while transferring?
fields.Fact: Lines starting with > are sent, < are received.

fields.Question: Which openssl subcommand opens a TLS connection and shows the certificate chain?
fields.Fact: Add -servername to send SNI.

fields.Question:
In this command, what does -servername set?
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com
fields.Aliases:
Server Name Indication
The SNI hostname
fields.Fact: Without it, a server hosting many sites may return the wrong certificate.

fields.Question: Which tool, usually run as nc, opens raw TCP or UDP connections?
fields.Fact: nc -zv host port is a quick port check.
